author.organization: Simula Metropolitan Centre for Digital Engineering

abstract.t: This document specifies the Nanoprobe Protocol (NPP), a lightweight, high-precision network latency and packet loss measurement protocol over the User Datagram Protocol (UDP). Nanoprobe is designed to minimize operating system and user-space scheduling jitter by leveraging Network Interface Controller (NIC) hardware transmit and receive timestamps, socket busy-polling, and dedicated thread-to-core pinning. The protocol supports unidirectional (forward and reverse) as well as concurrent bidirectional (duplex) probing modes, configurable inter-packet pacing and payload sizes, and custom per-packet probe schedules. This document describes the protocol architecture, session state transitions, wire packet formats, timestamp logging conventions, reference implementation, and Wireshark dissector support.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Accurate characterization of sub-millisecond and microsecond-scale network latency, delay variation (jitter), and packet loss requires a probing protocol that avoids operating system kernel-to-userspace wakeup latencies and protocol stack serialization overhead. Conventional network diagnostic utilities such as ICMP echo tools rely primarily on software timestamps captured in the kernel or user space, while multi-protocol throughput benchmarking suites introduce session management complexity that can perturb fine-grained latency measurements.

The Nanoprobe Protocol (NPP) addresses these requirements through a minimalist, single-socket UDP design coupled with Linux hardware timestamping (SO_TIMESTAMPING). Every UDP datagram carries a fixed 16-octet header containing a 64-bit sequence number and an 8-bit message type identifier, allowing both handshake control messages and measurement probe packets to share a uniform framing structure on a single UDP port (default port 10666).

Nanoprobe supports three measurement directions—forward (client-to-server), reverse (server-to-client), and duplex (simultaneous bidirectional probing)—as well as customizable probe schedules, selective echo ratios, and clock-drift compensation.

section.name: Terminology
section.t: This document uses the following terms:

ul.li: Client: The endpoint initiating a Nanoprobe measurement session by transmitting a connection request (SYN) containing test configuration options to the Server.

Server: The endpoint listening on the configured UDP port (default 10666), accepting a single active Client session, negotiating test parameters, and acting as either an echo responder or a probe generator depending on the negotiated direction.

Probe Sender: The endpoint actively generating PING probe packets according to a configured delay/size pair or probe schedule (the Client in forward mode, the Server in reverse mode, and both endpoints in duplex mode).
Probe Receiver: The endpoint receiving PING packets and optionally returning PONG echo replies.

Hardware Timestamp: A nanosecond-precision timestamp captured directly by the Network Interface Controller (NIC) physical layer upon frame transmission or reception and retrieved via the Linux socket ancillary data and error queue interfaces.
Probe Schedule: A comma-separated sequence of per-packet (delay, packet size) tuples used in place of uniform inter-packet spacing and fixed payload padding.

section.name: Conventions
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.name: Single-Socket UDP Architecture
section.t: Nanoprobe operates exclusively over the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) using a single bound UDP socket per endpoint (default UDP port 10666 on the Server). All control signaling (SYN, SYN-ACK, SYN-RST, FIN, FIN-ACK) and measurement traffic (PING, PONG) are multiplexed over this single UDP association:
section.artwork: +-----------------------+ +-----------------------+ | Client | | Server | | (Ephemeral UDP Port) | | (Default UDP 10666) | +-----------------------+ +-----------------------+ | Main / Send Thread |--- SYN (Options) --->| Handshake / Echo / | | Receive Thread |<-- SYN-ACK / RST ----| Send Thread | | TX Timestamp Thread |<== PING / PONG =====>| TX Timestamp Thread | | (NIC HW Timestamps) |--- FIN / FIN-ACK --->| (NIC HW Timestamps) | +-----------------------+ +-----------------------+
section.t: To achieve nanosecond timestamp fidelity without blocking the packet transmission path, each endpoint decouples transmit timestamp collection into a dedicated TX timestamp thread that reads looped-back outgoing frames and hardware timestamps from the socket's error queue (MSG_ERRQUEUE). Receive hardware timestamps are delivered in-band as ancillary control messages (SO_TIMESTAMPING) alongside each incoming UDP datagram. An optional software emulation mode replaces NIC hardware timestamps with CLOCK_REALTIME timestamps passed across an internal AF_UNIX datagram socket pair.

section.name: Operational Test Directions
section.t: During session establishment, the Client negotiates one of three test directions:

ol.li: Forward Mode (direction = 0): The Client acts as Probe Sender and transmits PING datagrams to the Server. The Server acts as Probe Receiver and echoes a PONG datagram for every pong_every-th received PING (when pong_every > 0). When finished, the Client initiates teardown with FIN.

Reverse Mode (direction = 1): Following completion of the SYN/SYN-ACK handshake, the Client and Server swap operational roles. The Client enters the echo loop while the Server pauses 1 second (to allow the Client to transition to receiver mode) and then acts as Probe Sender, transmitting PING datagrams governed by the negotiated options (or the Server's local probe schedule) and concluding with FIN/FIN-ACK.

Duplex Mode (direction = 2): Following the handshake, the Server transitions into a dual send/receive state and waits for the first PING from the Client. The Client pauses 1 second after receiving SYN-ACK and begins transmitting PING datagrams. Upon receiving the Client's first PING, the Server simultaneously begins transmitting its own independent stream of PING datagrams. In duplex mode, neither endpoint echoes PONG replies nor exchanges FIN/FIN-ACK packets; instead, each sender waits 1 second after completing its transmission loop before closing the session.

section.name: Measurement Session Lifecycle
section.t: A Nanoprobe measurement session progresses through three phases:

ol.li: Connection Establishment: The Client transmits a SYN packet (seq = 0) carrying its nanoprobe_client_opts structure. If no SYN-ACK is received, the Client retransmits SYN after 50 ms on the first retry and every 500 ms thereafter until acknowledged or timed out. Upon receiving a valid SYN, the Server validates and clamps out-of-range options, binds the session to the Client's source IPv4 address and UDP port, and replies with SYN-ACK. While a session is active, any SYN arriving from a different IPv4 address or UDP port is rejected with SYN-RST, whereas duplicate SYN packets from the connected peer trigger a SYN-ACK retransmission.

Probe Transmission and Echoing: The Probe Sender transmits PING packets with monotonically increasing sequence numbers starting at seq = 1. In forward and reverse modes, whenever pong_every > 0 and seq mod pong_every == 0, the Probe Receiver replies with a PONG packet echoing the triggering PING's sequence number.

Session Termination: In forward and reverse modes, after sending all scheduled PING packets (or upon expiration of the configured test duration or receipt of SIGINT), the Probe Sender transmits a FIN packet carrying seq = next_seq (one greater than the last PING sequence number). The Probe Sender retransmits FIN (50 ms after the first attempt, 500 ms thereafter) until the Probe Receiver responds with FIN-ACK echoing seq.

section.name: Protocol Message Formats
section.t: All Nanoprobe messages are binary-encoded and encapsulated directly inside UDP datagrams. All multi-byte integer fields MUST be encoded in little-endian byte order, regardless of the host CPU architecture.

section.name: Common Message Header
section.t: Every Nanoprobe UDP datagram begins with a fixed 16-octet header (struct nanoping_msg):

ul.li: Sequence Number (64 bits, unsigned integer, little-endian): Packet sequence number. Set to 0 for SYN, SYN-ACK, and SYN-RST; 1 through N for PING; echoed from the corresponding PING for PONG; set to N + 1 for FIN; and echoed from FIN for FIN-ACK.

li.t: Type (8 bits, unsigned integer): Identifies the wire message type:

ul.li: 1 (0x01): SYN (Connection Request)
2 (0x02): SYN-ACK (Connection Acknowledgment)
3 (0x03): SYN-RST (Connection Rejection)
5 (0x05): PING (Probe Request)
6 (0x06): PONG (Probe Echo Reply)
7 (0x07): FIN (Session Termination Request)
8 (0x08): FIN-ACK (Session Termination Acknowledgment)

li.t: Values 0 (msg_none) and 4 (msg_ping_wait) are internal implementation state constants and MUST NOT be transmitted on the wire.

ul.li: Reserved (56 bits / 7 octets): Alignment and reserved bytes. MUST be set to zero (0x00) on transmission and ignored on reception.

section.name: SYN, SYN-ACK, and SYN-RST Messages
section.t: The SYN message (Type 1) has a total UDP payload length of 44 octets, consisting of the 16-octet common header (seq = 0) followed by a 28-octet client options structure (struct nanoprobe_client_opts):

ul.li: Count (32 bits, unsigned integer, little-endian): Test duration in seconds (default 0, meaning unbounded unless interrupted or governed by a probe schedule). In reverse and duplex modes without a server probe schedule, the Server enforces the range [1, 3600].

Delay (32 bits, unsigned integer, little-endian): Inter-packet transmission interval in microseconds (default 100 us). In reverse and duplex modes without a server probe schedule, the Server enforces the range [0, 100000000].
PingPad (16 bits, unsigned integer, little-endian): Number of zero-filled padding octets appended after the 16-octet header in PING packets (valid range [0, 2048]).
PongPad (16 bits, unsigned integer, little-endian): Number of zero-filled padding octets appended after the 16-octet header in PONG packets (valid range [0, 2048]).

PongEvery (32 bits, unsigned integer, little-endian): Echo reply ratio (default 1). The Probe Receiver emits a PONG for every N-th PING packet where seq mod PongEvery == 0. A value of 0 disables PONG replies (unidirectional probe stream). Valid range [0, 1000000].

TimerType (32 bits, unsigned integer, little-endian): Pacing timer mechanism: 0 = sleep (usleep-based waiting), 1 = busy (active busy-wait loop over CLOCK_MONOTONIC). When unspecified by the user, busy is selected automatically for Delay <= 1000 us and sleep otherwise.
Direction (32 bits, unsigned integer, little-endian): Measurement direction: 0 = forward, 1 = reverse, 2 = duplex.

CompensateDrift (8 bits, boolean): Non-zero (1) if the Probe Sender compensates for scheduling overruns by preserving the nominal start schedule (next_start = current_start + delay); 0 otherwise (next_start = now when behind schedule).
Padding (24 bits / 3 octets): Trailing C structure alignment padding. MUST be set to zero (0x00).

section.t: The SYN-ACK (Type 2) and SYN-RST (Type 3) messages consist solely of the 16-octet common header with seq = 0 and no trailing payload.

section.name: PING and PONG Messages
section.t: The PING (Type 5) and PONG (Type 6) messages carry the 16-octet common header followed by a variable-length zero-filled padding payload of 0 to 2048 octets (MAX_PAD_BYTES):
Including the 20-octet IPv4 header and 8-octet UDP header, valid PING and PONG IPv4 packet lengths span from 44 octets (0 bytes padding) to 2092 octets (2048 bytes padding).

section.name: FIN and FIN-ACK Messages
section.t: The FIN (Type 7) and FIN-ACK (Type 8) messages consist solely of the 16-octet common header with no trailing payload. In FIN, the Sequence Number field carries N + 1 (where N is the sequence number of the final PING transmitted). In FIN-ACK, the Sequence Number field echoes the value received in FIN.

section.name: Hardware Timestamp Collection and Log Format
section.t: For each echoed probe exchange (seq >= 1), Nanoprobe captures up to four nanosecond timestamps:

ul.li: t0: Transmit timestamp of PING at the Probe Sender.
t1: Receive timestamp of PING at the Probe Receiver.
t2: Transmit timestamp of PONG at the Probe Receiver.
t3: Receive timestamp of PONG at the Probe Sender.

section.t: When CSV logging is enabled, each collected timestamp is recorded with columns seq,timestamp-idx,timestamp,size, where timestamp-idx is t0 through t3 (appended with direction tags cs for client-to-server or sc for server-to-client in duplex mode), timestamp is formatted as seconds.nanoseconds, and size reports the IPv4 datagram length (UDP payload length plus 28 octets for IPv4 and UDP headers).
From these timestamps, round-trip time (RTT) excluding receiver turnaround processing delay is computed as:
When endpoint clocks are synchronized (e.g., via IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol or GPS), one-way delays in each direction are directly obtained as:
section.artwork: D_forward = t1 - t0 D_reverse = t3 - t2

section.name: Probe Schedules
section.t: In addition to uniform periodic probing, a Probe Sender can load a comma-separated value (CSV) probe schedule file specifying an explicit sequence of packet transmissions. Each non-empty line in the CSV file defines two fields:

where delay_us is an unsigned 32-bit inter-packet delay in microseconds (applied after transmitting the packet) and packet_size_bytes is the target IPv4 packet size in octets (valid range [44, 2092], from which 44 octets of IPv4, UDP, and Nanoprobe headers are subtracted to determine PingPad). When a probe schedule is active, the Probe Sender transmits exactly one PING per schedule entry and then terminates the session.

section.name: Open Source Software Implementation
section.t: The reference implementation of Nanoprobe is written in C and distributed under the MIT License. It targets Linux systems supporting socket hardware timestamping (SIOCSHWTSTAMP and SO_TIMESTAMPING), interface binding (SO_BINDTODEVICE), busy polling (SO_BUSY_POLL), and POSIX thread CPU affinity pinning (pthread_setaffinity_np).

section.name: Wireshark Protocol Dissector
section.t: A Wireshark protocol dissector (packet-nanoprobe.c) decodes Nanoprobe messages over UDP. It registers UDP port 10666 by default with user-configurable port preferences and "Decode As" support, dissecting the 16-octet common header, the 28-octet SYN client options structure, and PING/PONG padding payloads in little-endian byte order.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: Nanoprobe is designed for controlled laboratory, data center, and research testbed environments. It does not implement cryptographic authentication, message integrity protection, or encryption.

In reverse and duplex modes, a single 44-octet SYN packet causes the Server to transmit a stream of UDP PING packets of up to 2092 octets per packet toward the source address of the SYN. If exposed to untrusted networks, an attacker using a spoofed source IP address could exploit a Nanoprobe server as a traffic amplification or reflection source. Although the Server enforces upper bounds on duration (CLIENT_MAX_COUNT = 3600 seconds), delay (CLIENT_MAX_DELAY = 100000000 microseconds), and padding (MAX_PAD_BYTES = 2048 octets), and restricts active sessions to a single peer at a time, Nanoprobe SHOULD NOT be exposed on public Internet interfaces without network-layer access controls (firewall filtering) or cryptographic encapsulation (such as IPsec or an encrypted VPN tunnel).

Furthermore, an on-path or off-path attacker who can guess or observe the active Client's source port and sequence number could inject forged FIN packets to prematurely terminate an active measurement run.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: Nanoprobe uses UDP port 10666 as its default server port, which is currently unassigned in the IANA "Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry" and configurable via command-line options on both Client and Server. This document makes no request for IANA action.
